options.text: The Pendleton Act required competitive examinations for classified federal posts
The Pendleton Act let any administration remove civil servants for political reasons
options.misconception: Believes the statute legalized partisan dismissal

options.text: The Pendleton Act fixed the salary scales of state and territorial legislatures
options.misconception: Confuses federal reform with state legislative pay

options.text: The Pendleton Act barred federal employees from joining any political organisation
options.misconception: Turns a protection into a blanket membership ban

questions.explanation: The 1883 Pendleton Act created a civil service board, competitive exams, and protection against removal for political reasons. Patronage, not party membership, was the target.
questions.hint: Think of the 1883 statute that created a federal board.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a separate-car law obliged the state to provide
questions.learningObjective: Explain the duty a separate-car law placed on the carrier
questions.stem: Red ink from an old bottle spoiled the page, so I rewrote the entry on a state separate-car law that obliged a railroad to furnish separate coaches for white and Black passengers.

answer.exemplar: The statute obliged the railroad to provide separate but equal accommodations: distinct coaches for the two races, and cars of equal quality, fittings, and service. The rail line had to be built out and the cars maintained at the company's own expense, and it could not refuse carriage because a passenger's race differed from the car's other occupants.

questions.explanation: The duty fell on the railroad to supply separate cars of equal quality and service. The law regulated accommodations rather than travel itself, so the question was what the company had to furnish.
questions.hint: Focus on what the company had to furnish to riders.

questions.topic: A lynching statute enforced by the bereaved
questions.learningObjective: Identify who was given the right to bring a lynching case
questions.stem: Meteor shower kept me up, and I used the watch hours to write down what the California lynching law of 1879 did, noting that the survivors of the murdered man were given the right to bring the case.

options.text: It made lynching punishable by a fine owed to the murdered person's survivors
It created a state police force empowered to arrest mob participants in counties
options.misconception: Believes the statute created an enforcement body

options.text: It required counties to build new jails to hold people awaiting trial
options.misconception: Misreads the statute as a jail building measure

options.text: It offered a standing bounty to any witness who named a member of the mob
options.misconception: Confuses the fine payable to the family with a witness bounty

questions.explanation: California made lynching punishable by fine, the money going to the victim's family, who could also sue the mob in a civil action. It gave the state no arrest power; enforcement fell to the bereaved.
questions.hint: The statute made the family the collector, not the police.

options.text: The steamship company carried the newcomer across the ocean under a contract ticket
options.misconception: Puts the carrier's role before the agent's

options.text: A recruiting agent in the sending country arranged the ticket and the terms of passage
A railroad sold the newcomer a through ticket from the port to the interior town
options.misconception: Treats the railroad as the first link in the chain

options.text: A local association in the receiving town found the newcomer work and lodging
options.misconception: Places the settlement agent at the start of the chain

questions.explanation: The agent's contract came first; the ship, the railroad and the local society all acted later in the chain. The agent recruited, the carrier transported, and the receiving community settled the arrival.

questions.topic: The categories an immigration restriction created
questions.learningObjective: Interpret what a schedule of permitted classes amounted to in practice

stimulus.body: The schedule named the travellers who might be admitted: merchants, teachers, students, travellers for business, and ministers. Every other worker was listed in a separate column headed excluded, and that column was the longer of the two.

questions.stem: Tea went cold on the table while I copied this extract from my logbook into tonight's entry, and then I wrote out what the schedule of permitted classes amounted to in practice.

options.text: It established a points system ranking each arrival by points earned for age and skill
options.misconception: Confuses a later quota system with class exemptions

options.text: It exempted every merchant and teacher of every nationality from all later restrictions
options.misconception: Overstates how broadly the exemptions applied

options.text: It converted a race-based bar into a class-based screen built around occupations and purposes
It required every excluded worker to carry a certificate issued by a Chinese merchant
options.misconception: Mixes in the later certificate of residence rule

questions.explanation: The schedule turned a blanket bar into a screen by class, admitting merchants, teachers, students and travellers while excluding laborers. Points and certificates belonged to later statutes.
questions.hint: Notice the two columns and what divides them.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The arithmetic of a national-origins quota
questions.learningObjective: Compute an annual quota from a census base and a stated percentage

stimulus.body: The table for that year gave every country its share of two per cent of the residents recorded there in the 1890 enumeration. The margin note said the figure was fixed for the decade and did not move as arrivals changed.

questions.stem: Frost on the lens cap, and I spent the cold hour working the quota table into the log: a country with a recorded foreign-born population of 120,000 in the 1890 count was allotted two percent of that base.

options.text: The country's quota was 2,400 but rose every year with the national population
options.misconception: Assumes the quota indexes the growing population

options.text: The country's quota was 120,000, since the base simply counted the residents already there
options.misconception: Treats the census base as the quota itself

options.text: The country's quota was 24,000, because the percentage applied to each decade in turn
options.misconception: Multiplies by ten when reading the percentage

options.text: The country's annual quota was 2,400 arrivals, fixed from the earlier census base

questions.explanation: Two percent of 120,000 is 2,400, and the quota was a fixed annual number computed from an earlier census rather than a running population. It neither equalled the base nor grew as the base population grew.
questions.hint: Two percent of 120,000 is 2,400.

options.misconception: Believes regulation meant nationalisation of the lines

options.text: Published tariffs and penalties against rebates, giving shippers stable filed rates
A fixed national speed limit for every passenger train running in the country
options.misconception: Confuses safety rules with rate regulation

options.text: A guarantee that every passenger fare was set by one national tariff schedule
options.misconception: Overstates uniformity; rates were filed, not uniform

questions.explanation: Federal control meant published rates the company had to obey, plus penalties for secret rebates. The government regulated the roads rather than buying them, and its rules covered rates and safety.
questions.hint: Regulation meant filed rates and enforcement, not ownership.

options.misconception: Turns protection from dismissal into a total ban

options.misconception: Confuses accommodation rules with route regulation

questions.learningObjective: Explain how the 1879 California lynching statute was made to work
questions.stem: Nails loosened in the mount, and I read aloud from the log how the 1879 California statute worked: a lynching became punishable by a fine, and the money was to go to the family of the person killed.

options.text: The fine was payable to the prosecutor as a penalty for official negligence
options.misconception: Invents a prosecutorial fee

options.text: The fine was payable to the county, and the family could petition the governor for clemency
options.misconception: Misstates who received the money

options.text: The fine was payable to the state treasury, funding a reward for each arrest made
options.misconception: Turns the fine into a reward fund

options.text: The fine was payable to the victim's family, who could also sue the participants in a civil action

questions.explanation: The fine went to the victim's family, who could also sue the mob in a civil action. The law priced the act against the participants rather than creating a police duty.
questions.hint: The money was owed to the survivors.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Agents, passage, and where newcomers went
questions.learningObjective: Explain how sponsorship shaped where newcomers settled
questions.stem: Rain drummed on the roof, and I described in the log how newcomers were placed: ticket agents sent word ahead to a family or a village, and the newcomer went where that word had already gone.

answer.exemplar: Placement ran through personal networks. The agent's ticket carried a name, and a family already established in a town or village asked for that relative to join them, so newcomers followed earlier migrants rather than a central office's plan. Settlement was thus determined by whom the agent had already contacted, which is why a few counties received nearly all of a given village's arrivals.

questions.explanation: Sponsors and kinship pulled newcomers to particular places, so early contacts shaped where later ones settled. Few arrivals were assigned centrally, which is why a few counties drew most of one village's migrants.
questions.hint: Follow the names in the letters.

options.text: The ship company's agent recorded his name on the passenger list for the crossing
options.misconception: Puts the shipping list ahead of the document check

options.text: He presented his certificate of residence to the collector of customs at the port
An immigration inspector put to him the questions printed on the official card
options.misconception: Puts the inspection before the document check

options.text: The steamship line received its fee for carrying him on the voyage
options.misconception: Puts payment before any inspection

questions.explanation: The certificate had to be produced and checked at the port before the inspector's card and any fee mattered, and the shipping list only recorded who was aboard.
questions.hint: Begin with the paper the traveller carried.

questions.topic: The arithmetic of a national-origins quota
questions.learningObjective: Compute a country's quota from its recorded residents and a percentage

stimulus.body: The column for that country read four per cent of the residents recorded in the 1910 enumeration. The note in the margin said the figure was fixed for the decade and did not rise when arrivals rose.

questions.stem: Birdsong before sunrise, and I transcribed the quota column I had worked out for the log: a country's recorded foreign-born residents were 45,000 in the 1910 count, and the statute allowed four percent of that base.

options.text: The annual quota works out to 180 arrivals, since the statute counted only the excess
options.misconception: Drops a digit by dividing in the wrong order

options.text: The annual quota works out to 4,500 arrivals, because ten per cent stands for one per cent
options.misconception: Misreads the percentage as tenths

options.text: The annual quota works out to 1,800 arrivals from that country
The annual quota works out to 45,000, the recorded base being the allowance itself
options.misconception: Equates the census base with the quota

questions.explanation: Four percent of 45,000 is 1,800, so the country's annual allowance was 1,800. The census figure was only a base, and the quota was a fixed number rather than a share of later arrivals.
questions.hint: Multiply 45,000 by four hundredths.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of the filed schedule rule for shippers

stimulus.body: I copied this from the statute book on the table: the commission required every common carrier to file a schedule of its rates, and any deviation from the filed schedule was held unlawful.

questions.stem: The kettle sang twice, and I wrote in the log what the filed-schedule rule was meant to accomplish, then turned to the question the entry raised for a shipper wanting a lower rate.

options.text: It allowed carriers to raise any rate they chose on sixty days notice to the commission
options.misconception: Turns the requirement into a right to set rates freely

options.text: It fixed one national price for every commodity carried between any two states
options.misconception: Turns filed rates into a single uniform tariff

options.text: It required carriers to file their routes and abandon competitive rate-cutting entirely
options.misconception: Misreads filing of rates as a ban on price competition

options.text: It ended secret rebates by making the rate the company had to charge the rate it had published

questions.explanation: The point was to end secret rebates: a carrier had to charge the rate it had published. The rule constrained how rates were made and applied, and it did not create one national price.
questions.hint: Think about secret discounts to favoured shippers.

questions.stem: A rag of cloud crossed the moon, and I set down the entry about how a dismissal letter that named no cause was answered by a federal reform, and what that reform did for men like him.

options.text: It restored the professor's chair by reversing every earlier removal from office
options.misconception: Imagines the reform as a general reinstatement

options.text: It created a classified service protected against removal for political reasons
It made dismissal by trustees unlawful in every state university
options.misconception: Overreaches a federal statute to state institutions

options.text: It required the government to hire only professors of political science
options.misconception: Invents a subject restriction on hiring

questions.explanation: A dismissal naming no cause looked like patronage, and the federal answer was a classified service protected against removal for political reasons. It did not reverse past dismissals or bind state trustees.
questions.hint: Ask what it did to future removals, not past ones.

questions.learningObjective: State the ground on which courts tested equal accommodations
questions.stem: Snow settled on the rail fence, and I copied the question into the log: when a state law required separate coaches, on what ground did the courts test whether the arrangement satisfied the law?

options.text: Whether the railroad had built the separate cars at its own expense
options.misconception: Turns construction cost into the legal test

options.text: Whether the separate cars were free of any fare difference that the company set
options.misconception: Reduces the test to pricing alone

options.text: Whether the separate cars were equal in furnishings, comforts, and service to the other cars
Whether the separate cars were of a standard length fixed by the commission
options.misconception: Confuses car dimensions with equality of treatment

questions.explanation: Courts asked whether the cars gave equal accommodations: comparable fittings, comforts and service. Cost and car length were details; equality of treatment was the measure.

options.misconception: Puts payment before the judgment

questions.explanation: The letter names two men and a town where their people already worked, showing an agent recruiting from a village for a known destination. That is a network of named requests, not a lottery or a state count.
questions.hint: Note the names and the town in the letter.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The categories an immigration restriction created
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the exempt classes of an exclusion schedule meant
questions.stem: The candle guttered, and I wrote out the meaning of the exempt classes listed in the schedule, and how merchants, teachers, students, and travellers came to be handled differently from the rest.

answer.exemplar: The schedule admitted people by what they were doing rather than by race alone. Merchants, teachers, students, ministers, and business travellers were exempt because they were not expected to compete with wage labour. The exemption carried its own tests, such as the merchant who actually handled cargo, and those tests shaped who travelled, how much money a passenger had to show, and how the classes were argued over in later statutes.

questions.explanation: The classes were defined by occupation and purpose of travel, so admission turned on what a person did rather than on race alone. Exemptions carried proof requirements, which shaped who actually qualified.
questions.hint: Think occupation and purpose, not nationality.

An older census was cheaper and quicker for the commission to compile and print

options.text: Older census counts were the only counts that could legally be published
options.misconception: Invents a publication rule

questions.explanation: An earlier census froze the numbers, holding the admitted total down and keeping new arrivals from enlarging later quotas. Cost and convenience were secondary; no rule forbade recent counts.
questions.hint: The base was fixed so the allowance could not grow.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The arithmetic of a national-origins quota
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a quota figure was calculated from a census base
questions.stem: Spring mud made the lane impassable, and I worked through the quota arithmetic in the log, showing how a percentage of an old census count produced a fixed yearly allowance.

answer.exemplar: The formula is a multiplication, not a share of what is actually arriving. Take the number of residents of a country recorded in the census chosen by the statute, multiply by the percentage the statute assigns to that decade, and the product is the country's quota for the year. The base never changes during the period, so a year of heavy arrivals does not raise the following year's allowance, and the allowance does not shrink either when arrivals fall short.

questions.explanation: The quota was the stated percentage of the recorded base, so a fixed number resulted for each year of the period. Arrivals neither raised it in the next year nor reduced it when they fell short.
questions.hint: Multiply the base, then hold the result.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A lynching statute enforced by the bereaved
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a law giving the family a suit could check mob violence
questions.stem: The garden hose tangled round the spade, and I explained in the log why a law that allowed the family to sue was thought to check mob violence, and what it did not do.

answer.exemplar: The reasoning was deterrent rather than prohibitory. A mob that killed could be made to pay, and the people with the strongest motive to bring the case were the survivors of the murdered, who were willing to spend money and time on it. The law therefore converted a costless killing into a costly one, and in that sense it checked the practice. It did not make the killing a crime in the ordinary sense, did not guarantee a conviction, and did not stop a crowd that was willing to pay the price or that was never identified.

questions.explanation: The law worked by making the mob pay a price and by giving the survivors a reason to pursue the case. It did not make the killing an ordinary crime, and it did not guarantee a conviction.
questions.hint: Deterrent, not prohibitive.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Agents, passage, and where newcomers went
questions.learningObjective: Infer from a copied letter who decided a newcomer's destination

stimulus.body: From the letter I copied: brother, I have asked the agent to send you a passage, and the agent says the berth is held until the spring. Go to the house of your uncle Vasko and he will know what work there is.

questions.stem: Sleet drove at the window, and I set the copied letter into the log, and I wrote what it shows about who decided where the newcomer would go.

options.text: The newcomer was expected to choose any town along the line that had a station
options.misconception: Makes the newcomer the chooser

options.text: The newcomer was expected to follow the family already there, so the destination was fixed by the letter
The agent was to assign the newcomer to a mine, a farm, or a mill as needed
options.misconception: Turns the letter into an agent's placement power

options.text: The newcomer was to wait for the spring before deciding to travel at all
options.misconception: Reads the season as a decision about the journey

questions.explanation: The letter points the newcomer to a relative and to the work found there, so the destination was settled by the family connection rather than by the traveller, the agent, or a season.
questions.hint: The uncle's house is the address.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The categories an immigration restriction created
questions.learningObjective: List the groups an exclusion schedule treated differently
questions.stem: A stranger waved from the lane, and I listed in the log which groups the exclusion schedule treated differently, and what the differences rested on.

options.text: Merchants, teachers, students, ministers and business travellers were handled as exempt classes
Every man, woman and child of the excluded race was treated alike in every respect
options.misconception: Ignores the class differences entirely

options.text: Travellers whose visit was temporary were distinguished from those expected to work
options.misconception: Turns a business class into a length-of-stay test

options.text: Lawful entry was made to turn on a passenger's ticket rather than a stated category
options.misconception: Makes the ticket the deciding fact

questions.explanation: The schedule drew distinctions by class, exempting merchants, teachers, students, ministers and business travellers. The differences rested on stated category, not on a ticket.
questions.hint: Classes, not tickets, made the difference.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The arithmetic of a national-origins quota
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a quota base was fixed from a census of residents
questions.stem: Cloud shadow crossed the field and I marked the entry, and I wrote the question: why did the framers compute quotas from a census of residents rather than from the number arriving?

options.text: Because the shipping records were kept in a language the framers could not read
options.misconception: Invents a translation obstacle

options.text: Because the census counted arrivals more accurately than any shipping record
options.misconception: Claims a counting advantage for the census

options.text: Because a fixed base kept the allowance steady, so each year's ceiling would not drift upward
Because the census figures were the only figures that could be printed in a statute
options.misconception: Invents a printing rule

questions.explanation: The point of a fixed base was stability: with the numbers set from an earlier count, the allowance would not drift up as arrivals increased. No counting advantage or printing rule explains the choice.
questions.hint: Fixed numbers, steady ceiling.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: What federal control of the railroads achieved
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a pamphlet clause about managing one's own affairs

stimulus.body: I copied this from the pamphlet: the companies of the country are to be permitted to manage their own affairs, provided that they shall not combine to defeat the law and shall file and observe the rates the law requires.

questions.stem: A gust of rain hit the window, and I read the pamphlet line into the log and asked what the sentence says about the reach of federal control.

options.text: That control removed the carriers' right to combine in any respect whatever
options.misconception: Reads a qualified prohibition as a total ban

options.text: That control reached the carriers' internal management and their daily operations
options.misconception: Overstates control into management

options.text: That control reached only passenger safety and touched nothing about price
options.misconception: Narrows control to safety alone

options.text: That control reached the carriers' conduct in pricing, not their ownership of the lines

questions.explanation: The sentence lets the companies manage their own affairs while barring combinations that defeat the law and requiring filed rates, so control reached pricing conduct, not ownership.
questions.hint: Pricing conduct, not ownership.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A dismissed professor and the terms of public service
questions.learningObjective: Identify the remedy a civil service commission could order
questions.stem: Wind shifted in the night, and I wrote in the log that a dismissed professor could ask the civil service board to review his removal, and I asked what the board could do.

options.text: Publish its opinion only, and the department was free to decline to follow it
options.misconception: Reduces the order to advice

options.text: Order the employee reinstated with back pay, and the employer had to obey the order
Prosecute the political party that had pressed for the dismissal in the first place
options.misconception: Gives the board a partisan prosecutions power

options.text: Raise the professor's salary to match what the market was paying others
options.misconception: Invents a pay-setting function

questions.explanation: The board could order reinstatement with back pay and the department had to comply, which is why the protection had teeth. It was not advisory, and it neither prosecuted parties nor set salaries.
questions.hint: Reinstatement with back pay, and obedience.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a separate-car law obliged the state to provide
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish separation in form from inequality in substance
questions.stem: The hinge needed oil, and I explained in the log the difference between a law that separated passengers and a law that separated them unequally.

answer.exemplar: Separation was not the same as inequality, and the difference turned on the fittings and the service rather than on the fact that the cars were different. If the cars for one race were dirtier, less comfortable, or less convenient, the law had been satisfied in name and broken in substance, and a court would say so. That is why the requirement of equal accommodations, not the requirement of separate cars, carried the weight of the decision.

questions.explanation: Separation in form was lawful only if the separate cars gave equal accommodations in comfort, fittings and service. A court looked at how the cars actually were, not at the label on the timetable.
questions.hint: Equality in substance, not on paper.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A lynching statute enforced by the bereaved
questions.learningObjective: List what critics said the lynching statute failed to achieve
questions.stem: Snow on the high ground, and I listed in the log what critics said the California lynching law failed to do, and what they agreed it did.

options.text: It did not make the killing itself an ordinary crime, nor guarantee a conviction
It did let the survivors bring the case, and that was the part believed to bite
It placed a federal officer in charge of every county where a mob acted
options.misconception: Invents a federal officer in each county

options.text: It removed the victim's family from the proceedings and barred their testimony
options.misconception: Says the family was excluded

questions.explanation: Critics agreed the law let the survivors sue, the part thought to bite, though it did not make the killing an ordinary crime or guarantee conviction. It installed no officer.
questions.hint: What the law could not promise.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Agents, passage, and where newcomers went
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a recruiting circular as evidence about the agent's business

stimulus.body: I copied this from the agent's circular: the agent has received instructions from the steamship company to book such persons only as have been named in a letter from a registered household, and to send the list to the office before the sailing.

questions.stem: Darkness came early that evening, and I read the circular into the log and asked what the rule about the registered household shows about the business the agent ran.

options.text: That the agent's business was chiefly the sale of household goods to the newcomers
options.misconception: Recasts the agent as a goods merchant

options.text: That the agent sold tickets to anyone who paid, and the letter was only a courtesy
options.misconception: Turns the letter into a formality

options.text: That the agent filled named tickets for households already in the business of receiving newcomers
That the office kept the list to check the newcomers' names for spelling
options.misconception: Reduces the list to a clerical check

questions.explanation: The circular shows the agent filling named tickets for households that already received newcomers, so the business ran on established connections, not on open sale or a goods trade.
questions.hint: Named tickets, established households.
